headings.title: Introduction to Tissues and Membranes
headings.content: The human body starts as a single fertilized egg, which divides and differentiates into trillions of cells. These cells do not work alone; they organize into cooperating groups called **tissues**. When multiple tissue types combine to perform a specific, complex duty, they form organs. Furthermore, flat sheets of pliable tissue that cover body surfaces, line internal cavities, and wrap around organs are known as **membranes**. Understanding how these structures form and interact is fundamental for nurses caring for patients in Nigerian hospitals, whether managing a simple skin laceration or a complex case of peritonitis.

headings.title: Types of Primary Body Tissues
headings.content:
Human tissues fall into four primary categories, each with distinct structural features and roles:

- **Epithelial tissue**: Covers body surfaces, lines hollow organs, and forms glands. It acts as a protective barrier against physical damage, pathogens, and fluid loss.
- **Connective tissue**: The most abundant tissue type. It binds structures together, provides structural support, stores energy reserves, and transports substances through blood.
- **Muscle tissue**: Composed of specialized cells that contract to generate force and body movement. It includes skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle.
- **Nervous tissue**: Consists of neurons and neuroglia. It detects changes in the internal and external environment and rapidly transmits electrical impulses for body coordination.

headings.title: Epithelial and Connective Tissue Properties
headings.content: Epithelial tissues are characterized by cellularity—they are packed tightly together with almost no extracellular matrix between them. They are **avascular**, meaning they lack blood vessels and rely on diffusion from underlying connective tissues for nutrients. Conversely, connective tissues feature abundant extracellular matrix produced by cells like fibroblasts. This matrix contains protein fibers such as collagen and elastin, suspended in a ground substance that can be fluid, gelatinous, or calcified as seen in bone.

headings.title: Classification and Functions of Body Membranes
headings.content:
Body membranes line cavities and cover surfaces. They are divided into two main categories: epithelial membranes and connective tissue membranes.

| Membrane Type | Subtype | Location & Function |
|---|---|---| 
| Epithelial | Cutaneous | The skin; protects the body from external hazards. |
| Epithelial | Mucous | Lines body cavities open to the exterior; secretes mucus for protection and lubrication. |
| Epithelial | Serous | Lines closed body cavities; secretes serous fluid to reduce friction between organs. |
| Connective | Synovial | Lines joint cavities; secretes synovial fluid to lubricate joint movement. |

headings.title: Tissue Repair and Healing
headings.content: When injury damages tissues, the body initiates repair through either regeneration or fibrosis. **Regeneration** replaces damaged tissue with the exact same cell type, restoring full normal function. **Fibrosis** involves the formation of scar tissue composed primarily of collagen fibers, which restores structural integrity but lacks the functional properties of the original tissue. Tissues with high mitotic rates, such as epithelial tissue, regenerate easily. In contrast, cardiac muscle and nervous tissue have limited capacity to regenerate and typically heal via fibrosis.

headings.title: Clinical Implications for Nursing Practice
headings.content: Knowledge of tissues and membranes directly guides nursing interventions. For instance, burns damage the **cutaneous membrane**, compromising fluid balance and infection defense. Nurses must monitor fluid shifts and maintain strict asepsis. Similarly, patients confined to bed are at high risk for pressure ulcers because sustained pressure disrupts blood supply to skin tissues. Regular repositioning relieves pressure and prevents tissue necrosis. Understanding mucous membrane health also guides respiratory suctioning and wound care techniques across various clinical wards.
